\chapter{The Mind and the Page}
\label{ch:bn-mind-and-page}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I think, understand, read and write in Bengali, hear the stem vowel rise whenever the -i ending arrives, and read the flapped \bn{ড়} that Sanskrit never needed.}

Say āmi likhi against se lekhe, run the chapter's four verbs back — bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā — say lekhāpôṛā with the flap in it, and explain that \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে} was never 'we will see' but 'a seeing will happen', because every -ā form is a noun too.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bhābā]{\bn{ভাবা} (bhābā) — \textquotedblleft{}to think,\textquotedblright{} and the verb it was built out of}

\label{lesson:BN-C08-bhaba}



\begin{quote}
You already have the verb \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit built \textquotedblleft{}to think\textquotedblright{} out of it, by a trick Bengali still uses every day.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{ভাবা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভাবা}} — \emph{bhābā} — \textbf{to think}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{ভাবি} (\emph{āmi bhābi}), \textquotedblleft{}I think.\textquotedblright{} \bn{আপনি} \bn{ভাবেন} (\emph{āpni bhāben}), respectfully.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{ভাবা}} is \textbf{\bn{ভা}} (\emph{bhā}) + \textbf{\bn{বা}} (\emph{bā}). \textbf{\bn{ভ}} is \emph{bh}, a \emph{b} with breath behind it; \textbf{\bn{ব}} is the plain \emph{b} underneath. Two letters, one puff of air between them.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{ভাবা}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{ভাবয়তি}} (\emph{bhāvayati}), and \emph{bhāvayati} is not its own verb: it is \textbf{\bn{হওয়া}}'s verb with a gear changed. \emph{Bhavati} is \textquotedblleft{}it becomes\textquotedblright{}; \emph{bhāvayati} is \textquotedblleft{}he \textbf{makes} it become\textquotedblright{} — and from making-something-be to imagining it is one short step. So Bengali \emph{bhābi} and Bengali \emph{hôi} are one root, √\bn{ভূ} (\emph{√bhū}), which is also English \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}, Latin \emph{futūrus} (English \textbf{future}), and Greek \emph{phúsis} (English \textbf{physics}). The noun \emph{bhāva}, \textquotedblleft{}a state of mind,\textquotedblright{} sits between them: thinking is holding a state.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the gear that makes someone else do it}]
Sanskrit changed that gear with a lengthened vowel. Bengali changes it with the ending \textbf{-\bn{আনো}} (\emph{-āno}), and it is completely alive:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{plain verb} & \textbf{the made-to-happen verb} \\
\midrule
\bn{দেখা} (\emph{dækhā}), to see & \bn{দেখানো} (\emph{dækhāno}), to \textbf{show} — make see \\
\bn{খাওয়া} (\emph{khāwā}), to eat & \bn{খাওয়ানো} (\emph{khāwāno}), to \textbf{feed} — make eat \\
\bn{করা} (\emph{kôrā}), to do & \bn{করানো} (\emph{kôrāno}), to have it done \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One suffix, and a verb you already own becomes a verb about making someone else do it. There is no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}show\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}feed\textquotedblright{} to learn; there is a gear. That is the same machinery that built \bn{ভাবা} itself, two thousand years earlier and one language back.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhābā\textquotedblright{} — think — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi bhābi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the be-verb it was built from — \textquotedblleft{}hôwā … āmi hôi\textquotedblright{}
  \item see, then make-see — \textquotedblleft{}dækhā … dækhāno\textquotedblright{} — and eat, then feed — \textquotedblleft{}khāwā … khāwāno\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb from last chapter shares \bn{ভাবা}'s root? (\textbf{\bn{হওয়া}} — both are √bhū; thinking is making something be.) What does \textbf{-\bn{আনো}} do to a verb? (\textbf{Hands the doing to someone else} — \bn{দেখা} \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} becomes \bn{দেখানো} \textquotedblleft{}show.\textquotedblright{}) Give the Bengali for \textquotedblleft{}show.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\bn{দেখানো}}, \emph{dækhāno}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bojhā]{\bn{বোঝা} (bojhā) — \textquotedblleft{}to understand,\textquotedblright{} the third knowing}

\label{lesson:BN-C08-bojha}



\begin{quote}
Last chapter split \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} in two. This verb makes it three — and it plays the vowel game you already met, but this time the page tells you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{বোঝা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বোঝা}} — \emph{bojhā} — \textbf{to understand}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{বুঝি} (\emph{āmi bujhi}), \textquotedblleft{}I understand.\textquotedblright{} Look again at that vowel: not \emph{bojhi}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{বোঝা}} is \textbf{\bn{বো}} (\emph{bo}) + \textbf{\bn{ঝা}} (\emph{jhā}). \textbf{\bn{ঝ}} is \emph{jh}, the breathy partner of \textbf{\bn{জ}} — the \emph{j} you met in \bn{জানা}. And \textbf{\bn{বো}} is the plain \textbf{\bn{ব}} of \bn{ভাবা} wearing the \emph{o}-sign \textbf{\bn{ো}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{বোঝা}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{বুধ্}} (\emph{√budh}), \textquotedblleft{}to wake up, to notice\textquotedblright{} — the root that gave a prince his title: the \textbf{Buddha} is \textquotedblleft{}the awakened one,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{bodhi} is the awakening. Understanding, in this family, is waking up to something.

Behind it is PIE \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}ewd\textsuperscript{h}-}, and English holds two of its children: \textbf{bid} and \textbf{forbid}, from Old English \emph{bēodan}, \textquotedblleft{}to announce, to command\textquotedblright{} — a bidding is something made known to you. Greek took \emph{peúthomai}, \textquotedblleft{}I learn by asking.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the harmony again, and this time you can see it}]
\bn{দেখা}'s rule was that the \emph{-i} of \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} closes the stem vowel while the spelling stands still. Here is the same rule on a different vowel — and the spelling moves with it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\bn{আমি} \bn{বুঝি} & \emph{bujhi} — the \emph{-i} raises \textbf{\bn{ো}} to \textbf{\bn{ু}} \\
\bn{সে} \bn{বোঝে} & \emph{bojhe} — stays \emph{o} \\
\bn{তুমি} \bn{বোঝো} & \emph{bojho} — stays \emph{o} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same law as \emph{dekhi} against \emph{dækhe}: the high \emph{-i} pulls the stem vowel up after it. Bengali simply chose to write this one down.

And now three knowings where English has one: \textbf{\bn{জানা}} for a fact, \textbf{\bn{চেনা}} for a person, \textbf{\bn{বোঝা}} for the thing that finally lands. \bn{ভাবা} is the turning-over; \bn{বোঝা} is when it arrives.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bojhā\textquotedblright{} — understand — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi bujhi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair, then the older pair — \textquotedblleft{}bujhi … bojhe\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}dekhi … dækhe\textquotedblright{}
  \item think, then understand — \textquotedblleft{}āmi bhābi … āmi bujhi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three knowings — \textquotedblleft{}jānā … chenā … bojhā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is it \emph{bujhi} and not \emph{bojhi}? (\textbf{The \emph{-i} ending raises the stem vowel} — the same harmony as \emph{dekhi} against \emph{dækhe}, only written down this time.) Which of the three knowings would you use of a person? (\textbf{\bn{চেনা}} — \bn{জানা} is for facts, \bn{বোঝা} for grasping.) Which awakened prince is named from this root? (\textbf{The Buddha} — √budh, \textquotedblleft{}to wake.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pôṛā]{\bn{পড়া} (pôṛā) — \textquotedblleft{}to read,\textquotedblright{} and a letter Sanskrit never needed}

\label{lesson:BN-C08-pora}



\begin{quote}
This word carries a consonant Sanskrit did not have. It is the sound of a whole family of words wearing down, and once you hear it you will meet it everywhere.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{পড়া}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{পড়া}} — \emph{pôṛā} — \textbf{to read, to study}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{পড়ি} (\emph{āmi poṛi}), \textquotedblleft{}I read.\textquotedblright{} \bn{সে} \bn{পড়ে} (\emph{se pôṛe}), \textquotedblleft{}he reads.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{পড়া}} is \textbf{\bn{প}} (\emph{pô}) + \textbf{\bn{ড়া}} (\emph{ṛā}). \textbf{\bn{প}} is a plain \emph{p}. \textbf{\bn{ড়}} is \textbf{\bn{ড}} (\emph{ḍ}) with a dot underneath, and the dot changes everything: it is not a \emph{d} at all but a \textbf{flap} — curl the tongue back and flick it forward once, as in the middle of an American \emph{ladder}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{পড়া}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{পঠ্}} (\emph{√paṭh}), \textquotedblleft{}to recite aloud\textquotedblright{} — reading was reading \emph{out}, which is why \bn{পড়া} still covers studying as well as reading. And \emph{paṭhati} became \emph{pôṛe} by a rule that runs through the whole language: \textbf{a single retroflex stop between two vowels softens into the flap \bn{ড়}}. That is why the letter exists; Sanskrit, which never softened them, had no use for it.

Watch it swallow a second verb whole. Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{পত্}} (\emph{√pat}), \textquotedblleft{}to fall,\textquotedblright{} went the same road — \emph{patati} $\to$ \emph{pôṛe} — so Bengali's \textquotedblleft{}he reads\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}he falls\textquotedblright{} are now spelled and said alike, and only the sentence tells them apart. Past Sanskrit, \emph{paṭh} goes cold: no secure Indo-European pedigree, and none will be invented for it. The falling twin is the rich one — PIE \emph{*peth\textsubscript{2}-} gave Greek \emph{ptérón}, \textquotedblleft{}wing\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{pterodactyl}, \textbf{helicopter}), Latin \emph{petere}, \textquotedblleft{}to make for\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{petition}, \textbf{appetite}), and English \textbf{feather}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the harmony, on a third vowel}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\bn{আমি} \bn{পড়ি} & \emph{poṛi} — the \emph{-i} lifts the vowel \\
\bn{সে} \bn{পড়ে} & \emph{pôṛe} — the open inherent vowel stands \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Third verb, third pair, one law: the high \emph{-i} of \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} pulls the stem vowel up after it. \bn{দেখি} against \bn{দেখে}, \bn{বুঝি} against \bn{বোঝে}, \bn{পড়ি} against \bn{পড়ে}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pôṛā\textquotedblright{} — read — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi poṛi,\textquotedblright{} flapping the \bn{ড়}
  \item the three pairs — \textquotedblleft{}dekhi … dækhe,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}bujhi … bojhe,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}poṛi … pôṛe\textquotedblright{}
  \item read it, think about it, understand it — \textquotedblleft{}poṛi … bhābi … bujhi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the dot under \textbf{\bn{ড়}} telling you to do? (\textbf{Flap it} — curl the tongue back and flick, not a \emph{d}.) Which two Sanskrit verbs both arrived at \bn{পড়া}? (\textbf{√paṭh} \textquotedblleft{}recite\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{√pat} \textquotedblleft{}fall\textquotedblright{} — the same softening ate both.) Does the reading twin have an English cousin? (\textbf{No} — the falling twin does: \emph{feather}, \emph{petition}, \emph{pterodactyl}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lekhā]{\bn{লেখা} (lekhā) — \textquotedblleft{}to write,\textquotedblright{} and the noun hiding in every verb}

\label{lesson:BN-C08-lekha}



\begin{quote}
Four chapters ago you said \emph{dækhā hôbe} and were told it meant \textquotedblleft{}a seeing will happen.\textquotedblright{} This word explains why that was not a flourish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{লেখা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{লেখা}} — \emph{lekhā} — \textbf{to write}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{লিখি} (\emph{āmi likhi}), \textquotedblleft{}I write.\textquotedblright{} \bn{সে} \bn{লেখে} (\emph{se lekhe}), \textquotedblleft{}he writes.\textquotedblright{} The harmony, written down as in \bn{বুঝি}: \emph{-i} lifts \textbf{\bn{ে}} to \textbf{\bn{ি}}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{লেখা}} is \textbf{\bn{লে}} (\emph{le}) + \textbf{\bn{খা}} (\emph{khā}). \textbf{\bn{ল}} is a clear \emph{l}; \textbf{\bn{খ}} the puffed \emph{kh} you own from \bn{খাওয়া}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{লেখা}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{লিখ্}} (\emph{√likh}) — and \emph{likh} does not mean \textquotedblleft{}write.\textquotedblright{} It means \textbf{to scratch, to engrave}. Which is what writing was.

Ask English the same. Latin \emph{scrībere}, behind \textbf{scribe}, also began as \textquotedblleft{}to scratch\textquotedblright{}; Germanic \emph{wrītan}, behind \textbf{write} itself, meant \textquotedblleft{}to score, to carve\textquotedblright{} — what you do to a rune-stick. Three unrelated roots, one picture. That is convergence, not kinship: \bn{লেখা} and \emph{write} are \textbf{not} cousins, and past Sanskrit \emph{likh} has no secure pedigree. The finding here is a shared idea, not a family tree.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the dictionary form is also a noun}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the same word} & \textbf{as a verb} & \textbf{as a noun} \\
\midrule
\bn{লেখা} & to write & a piece of writing \\
\bn{পড়া} & to read & study, homework \\
\bn{দেখা} & to see & a seeing, a meeting \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every \textbf{-\bn{া}} form you have met does this. That is what Chapter 4's \textbf{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} was: not \textquotedblleft{}we will see\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a seeing} will happen.\textquotedblright{} It also builds nouns straight out of verbs — \textbf{\bn{লেখাপড়া}} (\emph{lekhāpôṛā}), \textquotedblleft{}writing-reading,\textquotedblright{} is the ordinary word for \textbf{education}. And the causative from three lessons back still runs on top: \textbf{\bn{লেখানো}} (\emph{lekhāno}), \textquotedblleft{}to get something written.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lekhā\textquotedblright{} — write — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi likhi … se lekhe\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chapter's four — \textquotedblleft{}bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā\textquotedblright{}
  \item education, flapping the \bn{ড়} — \textquotedblleft{}lekhāpôṛā\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}lekhāno,\textquotedblright{} get it written
  \item the five you could already write — \textquotedblleft{}ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch\textquotedblright{} — and which one wears the chandrabindu
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \textbf{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} saying? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}A seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}} — \bn{দেখা} is a noun as much as a verb, and so is \bn{লেখা}.) Is \emph{write} a cousin of \bn{লেখা}? (\textbf{No} — both roots meant \textquotedblleft{}scratch,\textquotedblright{} which is coincidence.) What did \textbf{\bn{দুই}} keep that Hindi's \emph{do} flattened, who else in the east kept it, and did \emph{dv-} survive in anyone's everyday numeral? (\textbf{The -i after it}; Assamese, Odia and Nepali; and \textbf{no} — only re-borrowings like \textbf{\bn{দ্বার}} keep \emph{dv-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
